example.after: I built an attendance app.

lessons.title: Structure a project summary
lessons.summary: Explain what problem a project addresses, what you built, and who it is for.
learning_outcomes: State the problem in one sentence
Describe a concrete feature or approach

lessons.introduction: A useful project summary gives the listener a map: the problem, your approach, and the people the work is intended to help. Avoid claiming impact that you have not measured.

example.label: Example
example.before: It is an app with many useful features.
example.after: The app brings campus notices and student discussions into one place so students can find updates more easily.
example.explanation: The revised example names the product's purpose and intended users without claiming a measured outcome.

exercises.learning_outcome: Select the option that best addresses: Which opening gives the clearest problem statement?

exercises.prompt: Arrange these parts into a useful project-summary sequence.

tokens.label: The problem users face

exercises.explanation: Start with the problem, explain the approach, then identify the intended users.
exercises.learning_outcome: Arrange the parts to produce a clear response for: Arrange these parts into a useful project-summary sequence.

lessons.title: Connect ideas with cause and contrast
lessons.summary: Link decisions, reasons, and limitations cleanly using because, although, whereas, and so that.
learning_outcomes: Choose accurate cause, contrast, and purpose connectors
Combine two choppy ideas into one logical spoken sentence
Produce a clear trade-off sentence using contrast
lessons.method_note: Applies Nation's Language-Focused strand paired with Swain's Output Hypothesis: noticing how connectors work, then immediately producing your own.
lessons.introduction: Interviewers listen for how one idea connects to the next. Instead of chaining sentences with 'and then... and then...', one accurate connector ('because' for reason, 'although' for concession, 'so that' for purpose) shows clear thinking immediately.

example.label: Worked example
example.before: We chose SQLite. It is simple. It does not handle heavy concurrent writes.
example.after: We chose SQLite because it requires zero setup, although it is not built for heavy concurrent writes.
example.explanation: 'Because' introduces the reason; 'although' honestly acknowledges the limitation in one smooth sentence.

lessons.title: Trim clutter for crisp spoken sentences
lessons.summary: Replace bloated phrasing with direct subject-verb-object sentences that sound confident aloud.

lessons.introduction: When learners feel nervous, sentences grow longer and vaguer ('did the implementation of', 'in order to make sure that'). Direct verbs ('implemented', 'to ensure') cut speaking effort and make listeners remember your point.

lessons.title: Use conditionals for design trade-offs
lessons.summary: Answer 'What if…?' and 'What would you change?' interview questions with accurate conditional and modal verbs.

lessons.method_note: Forces syntactic encoding of hypothetical reasoning (Swain, 2005), preparing learners for live 'What if…?' follow-up questions.
lessons.introduction: Technical and HR interviewers love hypothetical questions: 'What if traffic grows 10×?' or 'What would you change if you rebuilt this?' Accurate conditionals separate real plans ('If users upload X, the API will reject it') from hypothetical improvements ('If I rebuilt this, I would add caching').

lessons.title: Signpost spoken answers for listeners
lessons.summary: Use natural verbal signposts so interviewers always know where you are in a 60-second explanation.
learning_outcomes: Open multi-part answers with a clear roadmap phrase
Signal transitions between problem, action, trade-off, and result
Close an answer cleanly instead of trailing off with 'so yeah'
lessons.method_note: Builds transferable spoken transition schemas so working memory focuses on technical content instead of searching for filler words.
lessons.introduction: Unlike a reader, a listener cannot skim backward. Brief verbal signposts ('There were two main constraints…', 'My specific role was…', 'The key trade-off was…', 'To wrap up…') act like headings in speech and eliminate awkward trailing endings.

example.label: Worked example

lessons.title: Build oral fluency with the 4/3/2 method
lessons.summary: Learn why repeating the exact same explanation under shrinking time limits eliminates hesitation.

lessons.introduction: Research by Paul Nation (1989) and de Jong & Perfetti (2011) proved one of the most reliable speaking-fluency techniques in second-language science: the 4/3/2 method. lessons.introduction: John Levis's Intelligibility Principle (2005) shows that listeners understand speakers best when word stress and rhythm are clear—regardless of regional accent. lessons.introduction: When the interviewer asks 'Do you have any questions for us?', saying 'No, I'm good' misses an easy chance to show genuine curiosity. Prepare two short, natural questions—one for engineers (testing, architecture, mentorship) and one for HR/managers (first 90 days, team culture).

example.label: Worked example
example.before: No questions, sir. When will I get my result?
example.after: Yes—what does a strong first 90 days look like for a junior engineer joining your team, and how are code reviews and mentorship structured?
example.explanation: Thoughtful, concrete, and focused on contributing well—not rehearsed flattery.

exercises.prompt: You are finishing a technical round with a Senior Backend Engineer. Which closing question fits best?

options.label: What is the biggest reliability or scaling challenge your team is working on right now?
How many paid holidays do we get in December?
Did I pass?

exercises.explanation: Asking an engineer about their current technical challenges sparks a genuine peer-level conversation.
exercises.learning_outcome: Select the clearest option for: You are finishing a technical round with a Senior Backend Engineer. Which closing question fits best?

exercises.prompt: You are finishing an HR/Manager round. Which closing question signals strong preparation?

options.label: What does your company do?
How does the team support onboarding for fresh graduates, and what habits help new engineers ramp up fastest here?
No questions at all.

exercises.explanation: Shows you care about ramping up effectively and learning team norms.
exercises.learning_outcome: Select the clearest option for: You are finishing an HR/Manager round. Which closing question signals strong preparation?

exercises.prompt: Write two closing questions you would genuinely ask at your next placement interview: one for a technical engineer and one for a hiring manager/HR.
exercises.placeholder: For an engineer:… For a manager/HR:…
exercises.guidance: Keep each question to one clear sentence so it sounds conversational, not scripted. Saved for self-review; not automatically graded.
exercises.learning_outcome: Produce pushed output addressing: Write two closing questions you would genuinely ask at your next placement interview: one for a technical engineer and one for a hiring manager/HR.
exercises.example_to_compare: For an engineer: How does your team balance shipping features quickly with automated testing and code reviews? For a manager: What distinguishes a junior engineer who thrives in their first six months on this team?

lessons.completion_condition: Complete all 3 exercises; open responses are saved for self-review rather than automatically graded.

levels.title: Foundation
levels.description: Start with clear, practical communication tasks. This is a curriculum stage, not a measured learner level.

levels.title: Developing
levels.description: Connect ideas across clauses, handle workplace scenarios, and explain technical trade-offs clearly. This is a curriculum stage, not a measured learner level.

levels.title: Placement-Ready
levels.description: Practise realistic interview depth, 4/3/2 compressed-time fluency drills, and calm recovery under follow-up probing. This is a curriculum stage, not a placement prediction.

units.title: Sentence foundations
units.description: Build, expand, combine, shorten, and clarify complete sentences.
learning_outcomes: Build complete sentences and organise ideas clearly
Expand, combine, shorten, and clarify sentences without changing their meaning

units.title: Grammar in context
units.description: Use verb tense, articles, prepositions, and question forms in context.
learning_outcomes: Use common verb forms, articles, and prepositions in context
Form clear questions and review common grammar errors

units.title: Vocabulary in context
units.description: Learn precise words, useful collocations, definitions, and phrases in study contexts.
learning_outcomes: Choose precise words and natural collocations
Understand useful phrases and create examples from personal study or project work

units.title: Listening for details
units.description: Follow short spoken updates and conversations using replay and accessible text alternatives.
learning_outcomes: Identify key details in short spoken updates
Follow requests, responses, and next actions in brief conversations

units.title: Project explanation structure
units.description: Explain the problem, approach, and intended users.
learning_outcomes: Explain a project problem, approach, and intended users
Organise a concise project summary

units.title: Evidence and clarity
units.description: Describe implementation and evidence without overclaiming.
learning_outcomes: Describe specific implementation and checks
Separate verified evidence from intended outcomes and remaining limitations

units.title: Starting point snapshot
units.description: Record a few current responses before choosing what to practise next.
learning_outcomes: Record current sentence, listening, and project-explanation responses
Keep a repeatable baseline without assigning a proficiency level

units.title: Speaking with structure
units.description: Practise short descriptions, explanations, retelling, opinions, and follow-up responses.
learning_outcomes: Describe, explain, and retell information in connected responses
Give an opinion with a reason and respond to follow-up questions

units.title: Listen, repeat, and self-review
units.description: Practise clear model phrases at a comfortable pace and reflect on what is easy to understand. No pronunciation score is generated.
learning_outcomes: Listen to model phrases and repeat at a comfortable pace
Choose a private self-review focus without receiving a pronunciation score

units.title: Workplace engineering communication
units.description: Practise crisp daily standups, constructive code reviews, and turning technical notes into concise spoken briefings.
learning_outcomes: Deliver structured 45-second daily standups covering Done, Next, and Blockers
Give and receive objective, code-focused pull-request feedback
Convert written engineering notes into Bottom-Line-Up-Front spoken updates

units.title: Stakeholders, scope, and live demos
units.description: Explain technical ideas to non-technical listeners, negotiate tight deadlines calmly, and lead a 3-minute demo or viva.
learning_outcomes: Translate backend and architecture trade-offs into plain user outcomes
Flag schedule risks early with tested options and a clear recommendation
Structure a 3-minute live demo and answer viva cross-questions cleanly

units.title: HR & behavioural mastery
units.description: Build an authentic 60-second self-introduction, 20/60/20 STAR stories, and calm answers to conflict and failure prompts.
learning_outcomes: Deliver a concise Present-Past-Future introduction without clichés
Structure behavioural answers with 60% focus on personal Action and real results
Discuss disagreements, mistakes, and weaknesses truthfully with growth evidence

units.title: Technical & CS explanation
units.description: Articulate data-structure trade-offs, database/API design, and live coding reasoning clearly aloud.
learning_outcomes: Compare data structures on time, space, ordering, and real use cases
Explain indexing trade-offs, transactions, and HTTP error semantics clearly
Narrate Clarify -> Brute Force -> Optimise -> Edge Cases aloud during coding rounds

units.title: Recovery, follow-ups, and closing
units.description: Stay composed when stumped, answer deep probing concisely, and close interviews with thoughtful questions.
learning_outcomes: Recover honestly when unsure without bluffing or shutting down
Answer targeted follow-up probes concisely without repeating earlier intros
Close interviews with genuine, role-tailored engineering and team questions
